chief_complaint: daily throbbing headache and whooshing sound in ears for 2 months
hpi_details: 2-month history of daily, severe, generalized throbbing headaches that are worse in the morning on waking and exacerbated by coughing, straining, or bending forward. Experiences a rhythmic whooshing noise in both ears synchronised with her heartbeat (pulsatile tinnitus). Reports transient 5-second episodes of complete visual darkening or grey-out (transient visual obscurations) triggered whenever she stands up quickly or bends over to tie her shoes. Gained 15kg over the past year.
ideas: thinks high blood pressure from her recent weight gain is causing pressure headaches
concerns: afraid she has a large brain tumour pressing on her optic nerves
expectations: wants a brain scan immediately and fluid tablets to drain the pressure behind her eyes
pmh: obesity (BMI 36), polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), mild acne
medications: combined oral contraceptive pill, minocycline 100mg OD for acne over past 4 months
social_hx: non-smoker, zero alcohol, administrative assistant, sedentary

investigation_events.title: Urgent intracranial pressure assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Urgent MRI/MRV and lumbar puncture results are now available. Lumbar puncture was performed only after imaging excluded a mass lesion and venous sinus thrombosis.

results.value: No mass, hydrocephalus, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; partially empty sella and bilateral transverse sinus narrowing

results.note: Measured in the lateral decubitus position; routine CSF constituents are normal.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Immediately discontinue offending medications (minocycline and oral contraceptive pill), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: daily throbbing headache and whooshing sound in ears for 2 months

Key HPI features: 2-month history of daily, severe, generalized throbbing headaches that are worse in the morning on waking and exacerbated by coughing, straining, or bending forward. Experiences a rhythmic whooshing noise in both ears synchronised with her heartbeat (pulsatile tinnitus). Reports transient 5-second episodes of complete visual darkening or grey-out (transient visual obscurations) triggered whenever she stands up quickly or bends over to tie her shoes. Gained 15kg over the past year.

Objective/Exam findings: Fundoscopy: bilateral grade IV papilloedema (blurred disc margins, loss of venous pulsations, peripapillary flame haemorrhages). Visual field testing: enlarged blind spots and early nasal step/peripheral constriction. Cranial nerve exam: check for bilateral VIth nerve palsy (false localizing sign of raised ICP causing horizontal diplopia). Urgent MRI Brain with MR Venography (normal brain parenchyma without mass/hydrocephalus; MRV rules out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and shows transverse sinus stenosis/empty sella). Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus position: opening pressure markedly elevated (>25 cm H2O, often >30-40 cm H2O) with completely normal CSF constituents.
Relevant background/PMH: obesity (BMI 36), polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), mild acne
Current medications: combined oral contraceptive pill, minocycline 100mg OD for acne over past 4 months
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any visual field loss or progression — optic nerve damage can become permanent.
management_principles: Immediately discontinue offending medications (minocycline and oral contraceptive pill)
Initiate carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide starting 500mg BID up-titrated up to 2g daily) to decrease CSF production
Urgent ophthalmology referral for regular visual field monitoring (critical instructions: permanent optic atrophy and blindness can occur if uncontrolled)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 26F with recent weight gain and minocycline/OCP exposure presents with signs of raised intracranial pressure: morning throbbing headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations on posture change.
reference_soap.objective: Fundoscopy: bilateral grade IV papilloedema (blurred disc margins, loss of venous pulsations, peripapillary flame haemorrhages). Visual field testing: enlarged blind spots and early nasal step/peripheral constriction. Cranial nerve exam: check for bilateral VIth nerve palsy (false localizing sign of raised ICP causing horizontal diplopia). Urgent MRI Brain with MR Venography (normal brain parenchyma without mass/hydrocephalus; MRV rules out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and shows transverse sinus stenosis/empty sella). Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus position: opening pressure markedly elevated (>25 cm H2O, often >30-40 cm H2O) with completely normal CSF constituents.
reference_soap.assessment: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri) likely exacerbated by minocycline and rapid weight gain. DDx: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), intracranial mass lesion, obstructive hydrocephalus, secondary intracranial hypertension from tetracyclines/retinoids.
reference_soap.plan: Immediately discontinue offending medications (minocycline and oral contraceptive pill). Initiate carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide starting 500mg BID up-titrated up to 2g daily) to decrease CSF production. Urgent ophthalmology referral for regular visual field monitoring (critical instructions: permanent optic atrophy and blindness can occur if uncontrolled). Structured multidisciplinary weight loss management (target 10-15% body weight reduction is curative in many cases). Neurosurgical referral for optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting if visual fields deteriorate despite medical therapy.

learning_objectives: Identify the classical symptom triad of raised intracranial pressure: morning headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations
Correlate epidemiological risk factors (young obese female) and drug exposures (tetracyclines, retinoids, contraceptives) with IIH pathogenesis
Explain the mandatory sequence of neuroimaging (MRI/MRV to exclude mass or venous sinus thrombosis) prior to diagnostic lumbar puncture
Emphasize the urgent priority of visual field monitoring to prevent irreversible optic atrophy

teaching.one_liner: Elevated pressure around the brain without a mass — typically in young obese women — causing daily morning headaches worse with straining, pulsatile tinnitus, and brief 'graying out' of vision on standing; untreated, it can cause permanent blindness.
red_flags: Any visual field loss or progression — optic nerve damage can become permanent

must_ask.say: Is the headache worse in the morning, and does it get worse when you cough or bend over?
Do you hear a whooshing sound in your ears that matches your heartbeat?
Do you have brief moments where your vision goes gray or dark, especially when standing up?
How much weight have you gained recently?
Are you taking any acne medications like minocycline, or birth control pills?

history.answer: I have had severe, throbbing headaches every single day for the past two months, and there is a loud whooshing sound in both of my ears.
It started gradually about two months ago rather than striking all at once, but it has steadily gotten more intense.
The headache happens every single day and lasts virtually all day long; I have never experienced anything like this before.
The pounding is generalized all over my head, but the heavy pressure feels worst directly behind both eyes.
It feels like a deep, rhythmic throbbing that reaches about an 8 out of 10 on my worst days.
It is distinctly worse right when I wake up in the morning, and it usually stays with me all day.
Coughing, straining on the toilet, or bending over to pick things up makes the pressure spike dramatically; resting quietly helps a tiny bit.
I hear a rhythmic rushing or whooshing noise in both ears that beats in exact time with my pulse.
Whenever I stand up quickly or bend over to tie my shoes, my vision completely greys out for about five seconds before coming back.
I do not have permanent vision loss, but sometimes I notice double vision when looking off to the sides.
I do not see flickering lights or shimmering jagged lines before the headache starts.
I get slightly sick to my stomach when the pain is severe, but I have not vomited, and bright lights bother me somewhat.
No, my eyes do not get red or watery, my nose is not runny, and my eyelids are not droopy.
I have had no fever, no chills, no neck stiffness, and no skin rashes.
I have not noticed any arm or leg weakness, numbness, slurred speech, confusion, or convulsions.
No, I have not had any falls, bumps, or head injuries recently.
I tried taking over-the-counter ibuprofen two or three times a week, but it did not provide any relief.
I have not noticed any triggers like skipping meals, specific foods, alcohol, or emotional stress.
I have never been told I have high blood pressure, and I do not take any blood pressure tablets or blood thinners.
No one else in my household has headaches, and our apartment has electric heating with no gas appliances.
I have never had cancer, HIV, or taken any medications that weaken the immune system.
I have gained about 15 kilograms over the past year because of my low activity level.
I wonder if gaining so much weight pushed my blood pressure up and caused fluid pressure to build up inside my head.
I am really frightened that there is a large brain tumor pressing directly on the nerves of my eyes.
I really want to get an urgent brain scan today and perhaps some water pills to relieve the swelling behind my eyes.
I have polycystic ovary syndrome, mild acne, and weight issues, but no other chronic health conditions.
I have never undergone any surgical procedures and have never been hospitalized.
I take minocycline 100 milligrams once a day for acne, which I started four months ago, and a combined birth control pill.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any vaping products.
I do not drink any alcohol at all.
I work as an administrative assistant sitting at a desk and live in an apartment with my partner.
My mother takes medicine for high blood pressure, but there is no family history of brain tumors, aneurysms, or chronic headaches.
My last period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular on the pill, and there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
The patient is alert, oriented, moderately uncomfortable due to headache, with visible central adiposity.

Fundoscopy reveals bilateral grade IV papilledema with blurred disc margins, loss of venous pulsations, and peripapillary flame hemorrhages; visual fields show enlarged blind spots and early nasal constriction.
Bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsy with reduced lateral gaze abduction and horizontal diplopia; all other cranial nerves are completely intact.
Supple neck without resistance to passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Full 5/5 muscle strength throughout all extremities with normal muscle bulk and tone.
Intact sensation to light touch, pinprick, and vibration symmetrically across all four extremities.
Biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles reflexes are 2+ bilaterally, and plantar responses are flexor.
Normal finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements; gait is steady and Romberg test is negative.
No tenderness elicited on palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary sinuses.
Normal external auditory canals and intact tympanic membranes bilaterally, with no audible bruit behind the ears.
